full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the pre-emptee is directed against the judgment of affirmance in a proceeding under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 The pre-emptor filed an application for pre-emption under section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for pre-empting plots 489 and 490 transferred by kabala dated 3.8.72 for a consideration of laka 3000/-. The said application was filed on 13.11.72 en the allegations inter alia that the preemptor is a tenant holding land contiguous to plot Nos. 489 and 490. He has no land contiguous to plot No 488 and as such he prayed for pre-emption of those plots only. 

 3. The learned Munsif en consideration of the materials en record allowed the application for pre-emption holding inter alia that there was no defect of parties since the persons left out had already been impleaded by the pre-emptor. According to the learned Munsif the instant claim for pre-emption was not hit by the rule against partial pre-emption and that the application did not suffer for insufficient deposit. The learned Munsif, however found that of the three plots transferred by the impugned kabala, the pre-emptor did not claim plot No. 488 since it was not contiguous to his land. Out of the two plots 482 and 490 the learned Munsif found that the pre-emptor was not a tenant holding land contiguous to plot 490 and therefore the pre-emptors claim was confined only in respect of the plot No. 489. In that view of the matter the learned Munsif allowed the pre-emption in respect of the plot No. 489 only, On appeal the learned Additional District Judge affirmed the decision of the learned Munsif holding inter alia that it was not a case of partial pre-emption and the deposit was in excess and as such the application was not liable to be dismissed on the ground of insufficient deposit. In reaching the above conclusion the learned Additional District Judge took into consideration the facts and surrounding circumstances of the case and also the material provisions of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The learned Additional District Judge on consideration of section 96(3) held that the deposit of "proportionate amount of consideration should be accepted as a sufficient deposit under sub-section (3) of section 96 of the same Act." 

 5. The other question centres around the expression "tenant or tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred," occurring in section 96(1) of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. According to Mr. Khan, the pre-emptor has no option to confine his claim to any part of the land transferred. In his view the pre-emptor should have applied for the entire land transferred as contained in the kabala dated 3.8.72. Mr. Khan has referred to the decision in the case of Makhanlal Nag and another vs. Reajuddin Sepal and others reported in 13 DLR page 323 and Salimuddin Mondal and others vs. Mohltosh Bisvvas reported in 14 D.L.R. page 797. These case are distinguishable from the facts and circumstances of the instant case. In the instant case three plots of land were transferred by the impugned kabala. The pre-emptor did not claim pre-emption in respect of one plot in the application itself. His claim with regard to another plot failed at trial and the claim succeeded only with regard to remaining one plot. In the circumstances it is evident that the preemptor abandoned one plot from his claim since according to him he was not a tenant holding land contiguous to the said plot No. 488. On merits he failed to prove that he was a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred so far as plot No. 490 was concerned. Accordingly the only plot in respect of which he succeeded was plot No. 489. The expression "holding land contiguous to the land transferred" appears to have been used in a generic sense. It is for the pre-emptor to prove in respect of what land he is a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred. It, therefore, appears that the right of pre-emption which accrues on the transfer is referable to the "land transferred". In the instant case the pre-emptor was found to be a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred only in respect of plot 489. It, therefore, appears that there was no partial pre-emption so far as the claim of the pre-emptor was concerned. 

 The relevant portion of section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act runs as follows - 

 6. It is evident from the above expression that a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred, may apply to the court for the holding or portion or share to be transferred to himself. In the instant case 3 separate plots of a holding were transferred by the kabala dated 3.8.72. The pre-emptor applied for pre-emption of plots 489 and 490. The pre-emptor was not found to be a tenant holding land contiguous to plot 490. According to the pre-emptor himself, he was not a tenant holding land contiguous to plot 488. It is difficult to conceive that the legislature intended to deprive a tenant of a right conferred upon him in expressed language enabling him to, pre-empt a portion of the land transferred. It is equally beyond comprehension that the legislature intended to thrust upon a tenant to pre-empt a portion of the land transferred to which he is not a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred. The contention of Mr. Khan that a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred my pre-empt all or none does not stand the scrutiny of the language expressly employed in the statute. Further the contention of Mr. Khan renders section 96(5)(b) nugatory. In the circumstances it appears from the scheme of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act taken as a whole that tenant or tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred, may apply for pre-emption for the whole or any portion as the case may be, of the land transferred provided other requirements of the statute are satisfied. 

 For the reasons stated above, the contentions of Mr. Khan are of no substance.
